I love Korean food, especially Kimchi and Tteokbokki but I can't help but think that South-Korean food has a bit too much seasoning and sweetness to the point it overpowers the natural flavors of the ingredients. I love Korean Chicken Feet or Dakbal, but after trying Chinese-style braised chicken feet I can't help but feel like that is the superior way to enjoy the dish. There is so much going on in the Korean version; it is sharp, spicy, zesty, sweet and almost has industrial levels of flavor for lack of a better word. It's still really good, but the Chinese version kind of had a perfect balance where about half the flavor came from the protein itself, a quarter came from the spices and another quarter from the preparation method. The Korean version is like 40% of the flavor comes from the unique ingredients, 50% from spices and 10% from preparation style. Either way, I'll keep eating all these foods but it's just an insight I had about the different philosophies in Korean and Chinese cuisine. If we are talking Japanese cuisine they are pretty purist so there will always be a strong focus on either the raw ingredient being used and it's freshness/quality or the process by which the dish is made, like Unagi for example.

海苔を見て回ったり、買ったりしたい方は、釜山の機張（キジャン）にある機張市場へ行ってみてください。  市場では海鮮定食をぜひ召し上がってみてください。アワビ粥もおいしいですし、蒸したズワイガニも絶品です。食後のホットクも格別です。  機張市場では、海藻や魚介類のお買い物も楽しめます。ただ、お値段は決して安くはありません。まずは市場全体をひと通り見て回ってから、買うものを決めるとよいと思います。  私の両親は釜山出身です。   🎄🌅🌠🌹🌈   If you’d like to browse and buy gim (dried seaweed), head to Gijang in Busan and visit Gijang Market.  While you’re there, enjoy a seafood set meal. The abalone porridge is also delicious, and the steamed snow crab is fantastic. For dessert, the hotteok (sweet Korean pancakes) is a real treat.  Gijang Market is a wonderful place to shop for seaweed and seafood, though the prices aren’t cheap. Be sure to look around the whole market before deciding what to buy.  My parents are from Busan.
